briefs.headline: IIP growth surges to 8% in August
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Industrial production rose 8% in Aug as against 4.7% expansion recorded a year ago, on account of robust growth in manufacturing and electricity sectors.
Sequentially also, industrial production witnessed acceleration from an upward revised figure of 7.4% in July, latest data released Monday showed. For the first five months of 2026-27, the index of industrial production grew 6.7%, compared with 4.2% a year ago.
Manufacturing , which has a weight of 76% in the index, grew 9% as 18 out of 23 industry groups witnessed an increase in output, led by motor vehicles, transport equipment, electricals, machinery equipment, computers, rubber and plastics.
Electricity and gas supply expanded 12.3% on account of higher temperature due to heat wave conditions. Electricity production from both conventional and renewable sources recorded double-digit growth in Aug. The newly added water supply, sewerage and waste management sector grew 6.3%. Activity in the mining and quarrying contracted -5.6% during the month.
In the use-based category -- capital goods (16.9%), intermediate goods (13.7%) and infra goods (12%) industries registered double-digit output, reflecting the impact of sustained public capex in the economy. 
Consumer durables, too, recorded 11.1% growth during the month.
Bank of Baroda chief economist Madan Sabnavis said revival in industrial growth is a positive sign as this has been witnessed in the last few months. "Growth in credit to industry has also been very high and broad-based, supporting the hypothesis of the sector recovering quite rapidly this year to contribute positively to overall growth," he added. ICRA Ratings chief economist Rahul Agrawal said IIP growth in July-Aug has averaged 7.7%, up from 6.2% in April-June quarter, which should partly offset the likely impact of margin pressure stemming from the renewed surge in global commodity prices, on the July-Sept growth.

briefs.headline: Suitability platform to assess NPS investors' risk appetite in works
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: To ensure regulatory guardrails around pension products while giving customers greater choice, Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority plans to roll out a suitability platform that will assess NPS subscribers' risk appetite and ask suitability-related questions before they select a scheme.
"Suitability and risk appetite is something that we are focusing on. All the NPS screens, whether with a pension fund, on a CRA platform or the NPS Trust platform, will ask people the right questions. Their final choice of scheme is their choice, but our job is to determine their risk appetite in a better way," PFRDA chairman S Ramann said.
Ramann said lifecycle products were one way of addressing suitability. NPS has four lifecycle variants based on risk appetite, with asset allocation automatically changing as the subscriber ages.
He was speaking at the launch of the NPS Preference Index Study 2026 by HDFC Pension. "The study shows that Indians are ageing, with average life expectancy at 78 years, while the average family size has declined to 4.4 members. Pension coverage, however, remains low at 17-18%," said Sriram Iyer, MD & CEO, HDFC Pension Fund Management.
The portion of respondents actively considering NPS for retirement rose six points to 59 from 2023, while among the drivers of savings, children's education lost ground to emergency savings.
Ramann said the higher EPF ceiling need not crowd out NPS, as employees can invest beyond it in other instruments. "Most corporates are giving their employees the option to put money into NPS through salary deductions," he said. He said long-term investors need diversified portfolios, with equity exposure benefiting those invested for at least 15 years. PFRDA has expanded NPS investments to REITs, InvITs and alternative investment funds.

briefs.headline: Growpital told to shut down by regulator
briefs.bodyText: MUMBAI: Markets regulator Sebi has ordered Growpital Platform, an unauthorised collective investment scheme (CIS) that had mobilised about Rs 192 crore to invest in agricultural farms for tax-free returns to investors, to wind up and return investors' money along with 12% interest. Twenty eight entities associated with Growpital have together been fined Rs 26.1 crore, while two entities have settled the case with Sebi after paying Rs 40.6 lakh. On Jan 29, 2024, Sebi had passed an interim order in this case, directing the noticees to desist from floating any CIS. A confirmatory order was passed on April 26, 2024. Since then, Sebi completed the investigation and issued show cause notices to 30 entities.

briefs.headline: As consumers go big on experiences, private equity follows
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Private equity (PE) money is chasing the events and experiences economy in India-think KKR's bet on ticketing and live entertainment platform BookMyShow or Blackstone's investment in an Indian Premier League (IPL) franchise. Young consumers are now driving household spends and they are allocating a big chunk of their budgets to experiences.
Consider this: at Travis Scott's Delhi concert last year, nearly 100,000 tickets were sold within minutes. That roughly translates into India spending almost Rs 100 crore within minutes on a cultural phenomenon, analysts at EY said. Investors want to latch on to this trend early and take a share of these emerging consumption spaces.
"Experiences over things are a mega-trend. This shift is happening across categories and segments. Consumption patterns of young people will never be the same as that of the previous generation," said Vikram Kumaraswamy, partner at L Catterton.
There are some numbers to substantiate the growing scale of the space-estimates by analysts at KPMG showed that the local live events and entertainment market touched Rs 13,600 crore (as of 2025). 
Riding on the cricket fan base, IPL ticket sales grew to about Rs 500 crore in 2025 from around Rs 120 crore in 2008, data sourced from investment bank Houlihan Lokey showed.
The broader commercial sports economy covering media rights, athlete endorsements, sponsorships and franchise revenues is pegged at Rs 18,864 crore. "In an era increasingly dominated by AI, screen fatigue, and algorithm-driven digital consumption, live sports and fitness ecosystems stand out as the ultimate non-replicable, experiential asset class, which is why institutional private equity is aggressively leaning in," said Sameer Jindal, MD at Houlihan Lokey.
For PE investors, that irreplaceable real-world emotional pull translates into rare pricing power, highly resilient linear/digital media rights, diversified stadium and merchandise monetisation and an enduring consumer moat against the digital noise, Jindal added.
It was a stellar 350% return made by CVC in four years by selling a majority stake in Gujarat Titans to Torrent Group that triggered fresh PE interest in IPL. "As our demography is changing and the whole social media world is creating a very different consumer response to everything... we as investors need to find the right opportunities to participate in and benefit from the underlying growth," said Narendra Ostawal, MD and head of India PE at Warburg Pincus.
Businesses linked to providing experiences will do better. Even firms having a play in the product side will try and associate their brands with experiences. For instance, a brand could promote healthy snacking during a sports event, said Kumaraswamy. L Catterton will invest in businesses building around propositions such as better home experiences, travel and fitness.
"The returns profile for new businesses are not that straightforward. The consumer acquisition cost is high. We have to make sure we invest in businesses that have the operating leverage to grow sustainably in the long-run," Kumaraswamy said.

briefs.headline: Safety, profitability top priorities: Air India CEO designate
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: "Safety, reliability, profitability and pursuing disciplined and sustainable growth." 
Air India
's CEO and MD (proposed) Tewolde Gebremariam on Monday set these priorities out for the struggling airline group in his first Town Hall with employees. Apart from widening losses, AI's safety practices and alleged lack of discipline among crew are under the scanner since last June's Ahmedabad crash and then the recent case of a badly rattled Phuket-Delhi flight whose pilot-in-command was subsequently sacked for failing dope test on arrival.
External environment is also tough - airspace closures (particularly Pakistan), rising crude prices, rupee's weakness and global uncertainty - which are common to all Indian carriers. Foreign airlines can overfly Pakistan.
Gebremariam, who is awaiting regulatory clearance to take over the role, said India's favourable demographics, strong economic growth, geographic position and large global diaspora provide a "unique foundation" for AI's future success. "These factors give us confidence that if we execute well and remain focused on our customers, AI can become not only one of the largest airlines in the world, but among the very best," the former top boss of Ethiopian Airlines, who successfully turned around that carrier, said.
He also pointed out the challenging environment and thanked the over 24,000 employees for the change the airline has seen since being taken over by Tata Group in Jan 2022. "Over the past four years, a great deal has been achieved. At the same time, there remains significant opportunity ahead of us. That is what makes this an exciting moment for AI and for all of us." Addressing basic issues without getting distracted by promises of a flashy makeover, Gebremariam set the priorities for the airline which is trying to regain flyers' faith.
Safety
That "would remain the airline's foremost priority and guiding principle.... every Air Indian has a role to play... people (be) empowered to speak up, raise concerns and report issues without hesitation. If you see something, say something. The stronger our reporting culture, the stronger our safety culture," Gebremariam said.
Reliability
"Our customers should remember AI for its reliability. They should be confident that flights will depart and arrive on time, baggage will travel with them and when disruptions occur, we should communicate transparently and recover quickly."
Improving financial performance
While acknowledging external factors have affected the airline's path to breakeven, he stressed AI cannot afford to lose focus on financial performance. "We must improve both revenue and cost performance... Every employee can contribute to savings, and those savings add up across an organisation of our scale."
Sustainable growth
"Growth is the oxygen of business. But growth must also be profitable and sustainable. We will pursue expansion in a disciplined manner and ensure our people, fleet and network are ready to support it."

briefs.headline: Proposal marks Tata Sons' 2nd attempt to avoid listing
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Weeks after 
Reserve Bank of India
 directed 
Tata Sons
 to comply with upper-layer NBFC-CIC norms, Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata has proposed merging two subsidiaries, Tata Electronics Systems (TES) and Tata Consulting Engineers (TCE), with the 109-year-old holding company to take it outside the RBI's regulatory ambit and avoid a public listing.
The proposal comes barely 11 days after the Tata Sons board expressed its preference for a listing to comply with RBI's upper-layer regulations for a core investment company (CIC) or non-banking financial company (NBFC). At the board meeting, Noel representing the majority shareholders had opposed a listing, arguing that alternative options should be explored.
Noel's present plan marks a departure from past restructuring moves, such as the demerger of TCS in 2004 into a separate entity. It would also shut the door on minority shareholder Shapoorji Pallonji Group's hopes of monetising its Tata Sons stake through an IPO. Noel has submitted the proposal to Tata Sons and RBI; their stance on the plan was not immediately clear.
F N Subedar, adviser to Tata Trusts and former Tata Sons company secretary, described the plan as a return to Tata Sons' historic structure.
Tata Sons had housed operating businesses such as TCS alongside being the group's holding company in the past, Subedar said. 
Tata Sons assumed NBFC-CIC status only after TCS was demerged.
Binoy Parikh, partner at Katalyst Advisors, said the proposal may not permanently resolve Tata Sons' regulatory status. If Tata Sons were to later list Tata Electronics Systems or Tata Consulting Engineers, or induct external investors into either business, it could be forced to demerge them. That could reduce operating revenues and potentially push Tata Sons back into the NBFC-CIC category, reviving the listing obligation. "The structure is essentially a toggle that can be switched on and off depending on the regulatory outcome sought at a given point," he said.
The proposal marks the group's second attempt to avoid a listing. In 2024, Tata Sons sought to exit RBI's upper-layer NBFC-CIC rules after substantially reducing debt. Earlier this month, the regulator rejected the request for deregistration and directed the company to comply with its norms.
RBI's principal business criteria for an NBFC require financial assets and financial income to account for more than 50% of a company's total assets and income respectively. The proposed merger would tilt Tata Sons' income mix towards operating revenue, causing it to fail one of the two tests and thus fall outside the NBFC framework, according to a restructuring expert. The transaction could also take Tata Sons outside the definition of a Core Investment Company (CIC), which requires at least 90% of net assets to comprise investments in group companies. Tata Sons' net assets are Rs 2 lakh crore. With operating assets from the merged entities coming onto its balance sheet, investments would fall below the 90% threshold, the expert said.
According to Tata Trusts, the merged entity would have had an operating revenue of Rs 1.05 lakh crore as of March 31, 2026, far in excess of its income of Rs 40,072 crore from financial assets. Operating revenue would constitute 64% of the total income of the merged entity.
Subedar said the latest proposal is significantly different from Tata Sons' earlier attempt to exit the RBI's regulatory framework. "Earlier, we said we would remain a CIC. Now we are saying we would be neither an NBFC nor a CIC. That is the change," he said.
Noel did not require fresh approval from the Tata Trusts boards to pursue the proposal, Subedar said. He was acting on a unanimous July 2025 resolution directing that all efforts be made to preserve Tata Sons' status as an unlisted private company.
People familiar with the matter, however, disputed that interpretation. They said the July 2025 resolution cannot be automatically carried forward because the trustees' positions have since diverged, with the Trusts' two vice-chairmen backing a public listing of Tata Sons. They also said that when the resolution was passed, RBI had not yet ruled on Tata Sons' March 2024 application seeking an exit from the NBFC-CIC framework, materially altering the circumstances under which the mandate was given.
The scheme would require RBI's no-objection certificate before it is placed before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) for approval. It would also need shareholder approval, including the backing of at least 75% of votes cast.

briefs.headline: D-Street sees red as Gulf crisis, poor monsoon cloud outlook
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Thanks partially to Monday's sell-off on Dalal Street, the stock price of recently listed NSE slid below its IPO price for the first time and closed at that level. With foreign funds leading the day's sell-off, 
sensex
 lost 1,124 points (1.5%) to close at 72,771 points, nearly a six-month low level. And on NSE, 
Nifty
 lost 360 points (1.6%) to close at 22,780 points, also its lowest close since March 30 this year.
A host of factors led to the day's slide in the market. The rupee neared the 96-per-dollar mark again, while Brent crude spiked to near the $100/barrel level, after signs of escalation of the war in the Persian Gulf region emerged. On the domestic front, the impact of a weak monsoon pushing up inflation, interest rates and bond yields also weighed on investor sentiment, market players said.
In Monday's market, on BSE the stock price of NSE opened just a tad above its IPO price of Rs 1,785, dipped to an intraday low of Rs 1,761 and closed at Rs 1,763, down 1.7% on the day. On the day of listing, Sept 24, the stock had touched an intraday high of Rs 1,878 and has been on a gradual slide since.
In the broader market, the two benchmark indices were weighed down by weak global cues, elevated crude oil prices and bond yields, persistent foreign fund selling and heightened geopolitical uncertainty following the stalemate in the US-Iran peace talks, said Pabitro Mukherjee, deputy vice president-research, Bajaj Broking.The slide in the market came mainly on the back of a Rs 5,353-crore net selling by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) in stocks alone.
 Although domestic funds, with a net buying figure of Rs 5,189 crore, nearly matched the selling by foreign players, it was not enough to fully cushion the pressure.
As a result, investors' wealth lost during the day was at about Rs 7.5 lakh crore, with the market capitalisation of companies listed on BSE now at Rs 474.4 lakh crore, exchange data showed.
In the international market, Brent rallied 2.2% on Monday while on Friday, the Indian crude basket was priced at nearly $121 a barrel. In comparison, in April, at the height of the war in West Asia, it had hit a high of $114.5.
Rising crude prices are now threatening the domestic inflation rate, pushing up yields on Indian govt bonds and also having an adverse effect on the rupee.

stories.headline: How Anushka’s chole bhature search for Virat Kohli changed this Mumbai shop’s fate
stories.deck: A small chole bhature shop in Mumbai was on the brink of closure due to massive debts. After a comedian's Instagram recommendation, the business experienced sudden popularity and went viral. An order from Anushka Sharma for Virat Kohli further boosted their visibility and customer base. The brothers quickly expanded from one outlet to four as demand surged significantly.
stories.bodyText:
A small chole bhature shop in Mumbai that was once preparing to shut down after piling up nearly Rs1.8 million in debt is now serving around 3,000 plates a day and claims to generate nearly Rs20 million in monthly sales.
For Delhi Se, a tiny 250-square-foot outlet in Chembur, the remarkable turnaround began with an unexpected Instagram recommendation from stand-up comedian Abhishek Upmanyu and eventually involved an order from 
Anushka Sharma
’s home for 
Virat Kohli
.
The business was being run by brothers Jaspal Singh Khalsa and Mahinder Singh Khalsa, who had just three tables and nine seats at their outlet. Things had started going downhill in January 2022, and by September, the brothers were carrying nearly Rs1.8 million in debt.
“We were planning to close the restaurant,” Jaspal told Pinkvilla.
The brothers were preparing to settle their outstanding grocery bills and rent before shutting the shop for good. Then, on September 13, 2022, an unexpected customer walked through the door.
The Instagram story that changed everything
Stand-up comedian Abhishek Upmanyu visited the Chembur outlet, tried its chole bhature and recommended the food on Instagram.
At the time, the brothers did not know who he was.
“We didn’t know him then. On September 14 and 15, our walk-ins started increasing,” Jaspal recalled.
That recommendation would soon lead to something far bigger.
The Instagram post eventually reached 
Anushka
 Sharma, who was looking for authentic Delhi-style chole bhature in Mumbai for Virat Kohli.
Before Anushka publicly spoke about the restaurant, however, the brothers began receiving repeated calls from a woman claiming to be from her home. She wanted two plates delivered to Juhu and also asked for the restaurant’s bank details.
Jaspal thought something was wrong.
“I told Mahinder, ‘This woman is troubling me. She has called eight times and is asking for my bank details.’ Mahinder said, ‘What’s the problem? Give her the bank details.’ I said, ‘What if she hacks the account?’ Mahinder replied, ‘The account balance is already negative. There is hardly any money in it,’” Jaspal recalled.
After several calls, the brothers finally learnt that the order was genuinely from Virat Kohli’s home.
Even then, Jaspal struggled to believe it.
“I said, ‘Ma’am, please don’t say things like that. Where is Virat Kohli and where am I – a small chole bhature shop in Chembur? How am I supposed to believe that you’re calling from Virat Kohli’s house?’” Jaspal said.
Anushka Sharma post brings an instant crowd
The mystery was soon cleared up when Anushka posted on Instagram that she had finally found “ekdum-Delhi-jaise-Chole-bhature” in Mumbai. She also credited Upmanyu for pointing her towards the eatery.
The response was almost instantaneous.
“After her post, there was a massive crowd at the restaurant. Within half an hour, such a huge crowd had gathered that we were completely blank,” Jaspal said.
The three-table outlet suddenly found itself dealing with a rush it was nowhere near equipped to handle. Customers started placing orders for six or even 10 plates at a time, while the restaurant rapidly ran out of stock.
The crowd outside became so large that police reportedly arrived at the spot.
With demand far exceeding their preparations, the brothers began sourcing soaked chickpeas from neighbours to keep the kitchen running. Some customers reportedly waited for more than two hours to get just two or three plates.
The scale of the operation changed dramatically within days. According to Jaspal, the quantity of chole being prepared increased from around 8kg to 100kg within three days.
From a nine-seat shop to four outlets
The sudden attention turned what was once a struggling neighbourhood outlet into the foundation of a much larger business.
Delhi Se has since expanded from the original Chembur shop to four outlets spread across Mumbai and Navi Mumbai.
The owners now claim that the brand sells approximately 3,000 plates of chole bhature every day. Around 125kg of chickpeas are soaked daily, with the quantity increasing significantly after cooking.
The financial numbers have changed just as dramatically.
When the business was struggling, monthly sales were around Rs100,000–150,000 and the brothers were barely breaking even. Today, they claim monthly sales of approximately Rs20 million.
What began as a tiny nine-seat restaurant preparing to close was transformed by a chain of events the brothers could hardly have anticipated: a comedian’s Instagram recommendation, a search for authentic Delhi-style chole bhature and an order from Virat Kohli’s home.

stories.headline: Olympiad medallist Nihal replies to 'play for Pakistan' troll with 3 words
stories.deck: Nihal Sarin responded to an X user who told him to “play for Pakistan” after India’s Open team won silver at the Chess Olympiad, replying simply, “on board 0?” Nihal’s tournament was mixed, with five points from nine games after a strong start and two consecutive losses in the middle. India finished runners-up to Uzbekistan.
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Indian grandmaster Nihal Sarin didn't need more than three words to shut down a troll on X. After India's open team wrapped up their campaign at the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand with a silver medal, Nihal posted a simple message of celebration, penning, "Happy to win silver for Team India. Congratulations to Uzbekistan."
It should have been an uncontroversial post. Instead, it drew an ugly reply from one user. "Plz quit playing for India. Play for Pakistan," the comment read, which has now been deleted.
Nihal didn't let it slide, nor did he engage at length. His response was just as brief as the provocation. The Kerala-born grandmaster wrote, "on board 0?"
A mixed personal campaign
The exchange came at the end of a tournament that had its own share of ups and downs for the 22-year-old chess star individually.
He started in fine form, winning his first three games, against Thailand, Indonesia and Italy, before the results cooled off with back-to-back draws against Spain and the Netherlands.
Round 6, against hosts Uzbekistan, proved to be the turning point. Nihal blundered his queen in a winning position against Nodirbek Yakubboev, a loss that visibly rattled him, he lost again the very next round, in a marathon 88-move battle against England's Luke McShane.
Those two defeats were the only blemishes on an otherwise solid campaign; Nihal steadied himself in the rounds that followed, drawing against Germany's Frederik Svane, beating Uzbekistan second team's Mukhammadzokhid Suyarov in Round 10, and closing out the tournament with a draw against Hungary's Benjamin Gledura.
The individual numbers, though, were always going to matter less than the team result. India's open side secured silver behind hosts Uzbekistan.

stories.headline: Chess Olympiad: Amazing performance, says Savitha
stories.deck: The 19-year-old Chennai WGM dazzles on her debut in the tournament
stories.bodyText:
It was all quiet at Terminal 4 of the airport here even a good 10 minutes before the members of the Indian chess teams walked out. In a jiffy, there was a small crowd which included well-wishers and fans, all wanting a now-mandatory selfie with the players.
For a change, the spotlight wasn’t on R. Praggnanandhaa and R. Vaishali but on B. Savitha Shri, the new kid on the block, who dazzled with an unbeaten, gold-medal winning run (nine points from 10 games) as the women’s team clinched bronze.
The 19-year-old Chennai WGM, picked as the reserve board player in her Olympiad debut, proved her worth in gold as she kept notching up victories. notched up one victory after the other. Her heroics proved invaluable and a draw in the final round against Georgia helped the team climb the podium.
“The win against Elnaz Kaliakhmet was my best match,” she said of the performance against Kazakhstan. “If I hadn’t won, we would have lost that match.”
“It was an amazing performance. After I started with four wins, I thought I should carry on the good form and contribute to the team’s cause,” said Savitha Shri, who thanked her teammates for their support and showing faith in her.

briefs.headline: 'Olympics sapna hai': Yashvir after ticking off Asian Games and CWG medal boxes
briefs.deck: Yashvir Singh secured his second major international medal of the year after winning silver in the men's javelin throw at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan. The Indian athlete produced a personal best of 85.72m with his final attempt but could not overtake Sri Lanka's Rumesh Pathirage for gold. Yashvir had earlier won bronze at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: The last throw has become familiar territory for Yashvir Singh.
At the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow earlier this year, Yashvir produced a stunning 85.41m with his final throw to win bronze.
Asian Games Full Coverage
 | 
Schedule
 | 
Medal Tally
On Monday at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium in Japan, he was again waiting for his last attempt with a medal already within reach.
Yashvir was in the silver medal position after five attempts, with 85.14m as his best throw. He needed more than 88.55m to overtake Sri Lanka's Rumesh Pathirage and take gold.
Another final throw
The pressure was familiar. The outcome was different.
Yashvir ran in, stretched his arm and launched his final effort. The javelin travelled 85.72m — a personal best — but it was not enough to move him past Pathirage.
He walked back with a smile and exchanged a high five with compatriot Rohit Yadav, who won bronze.
“The situation was the same in both events (laughs). I was stuck with the last throw both times. This time, a medal was guaranteed. That throw had won me a medal. Both times, it was a very nerve-racking situation. It was a do-or-die situation. 
I had decided that it was now or never,” Yashvir told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview from Japan.
'Grip slip ho rahi thi'
Yashvir felt the conditions added to the challenge.
“Pressure was there. The throws were coming out well, but I had hoped to produce an even better throw. However, the weather conditions were not good, and my grip was slipping, which made things difficult. There were also some technical flaws,” he said.
“There was also a slight difference in technique. I had worked on the mistakes I was making in my throws, but I still made a few mistakes today. I will focus on them going forward,” Yashvir said.
Back-to-back major medals
Yashvir and Rohit carried India's javelin hopes in the absence of reigning champion and two-time Olympic medallist 
Neeraj Chopra
, who withdrew from the 
Asian Games
 after suffering a late ligament injury.
For Yashvir, the silver meant medals at consecutive major international events after his bronze in Glasgow.
“I won a medal in Glasgow first, and now I have won silver. I am very happy about this. Neeraj bhaiya supported me a lot. The entire country, my father and my whole family supported me. I am here because of them,” he said.
'Olympics sapna hai'
The next target is already clear.
“Olympics sapna hai [The Olympics are a dream]. It is everyone's dream, and it is mine too. I want to correct my mistakes as soon as possible. I will try to fix the mistakes, improve further and deliver an even better performance next time. I will give my best going forward,” he said.

briefs.headline: Kazakh race walker's gold medal stripped at Asian Games for footwear breach
briefs.deck: Danzengquzong was upgraded to the gold, ⁠with compatriot Ma Li earning silver ahead of Japan's ‌bronze-winner Yukiko Umeno.
briefs.bodyText:
Kazakh race walker Yasmina Toxanbayeva's Asian Games gold medal has been annulled following disqualification from the women's marathon event for wearing unsanctioned shoes.
Toxanbayeva crossed first in the event on Sunday in three hours, 22 minutes and 20 seconds, nearly four minutes ahead of China's runner-up Danzengquzong, but the results remained provisional pending a protest.
"Athletes must wear only those shoes approved and listed on a World Athletics platform. She was not wearing one, which is why we wrote to World Athletics," a technical official said on Monday.
"Cancelling the gold was their decision, which we conveyed to the athlete. The athlete has a right to appeal to the jury, and she has done that."
Toxanbayeva confirmed the annulment on social media.
"We fought until the end," she said in an Instagram post. "Thank you to all my super-heroes who fought with me to the very end."
Danzengquzong was upgraded to the gold, with compatriot Ma Li earning silver ahead of Japan's bronze-winner Yukiko Umeno.

briefs.headline: Greece stun Germany 1-0 in losing home debut for Klopp
briefs.deck: It was the ⁠first ever victory for the Greeks in 11 matches against the Germans, and they now lead their group on six points from two matches. Germany are on one point.
briefs.bodyText:
Greece scored a 74th-minute goal through Dimitris Kourbelis to stun hosts Germany 1-0 in their Nations League Group A2 on Sunday to top the group and spoil coach Juergen Klopp’s home debut on the German bench.
It was the first ever victory for the Greeks in 11 matches against the Germans, and they now lead their group on six points from two matches. Germany are on one point.
The hosts were in control for most of the game and had close to 80% possession in the first half alone but they were ultimately punished for sloppy defending, especially in the second half, which gave the Greeks space to attack.
Klopp, who took over in July after Germany’s early World Cup exit, has now failed to win either of his two matches in charge following a 1-1 draw against the Dutch in Amsterdam on Thursday.
“I could have lived with us not winning but you cannot lose such a game,” Klopp said. “We have been together for a week now, all mixed together, and that needs time.
“The result is not cool but it is absolutely part of the process,” he said. Germany next play Serbia on Thursday before travelling to Greece three days later.
TWO WINS IN A ROW FOR GREECE
Despite enjoying a dominant first half it was only after they upped their tempo and started pressing higher that Germany carved out scoring chances.
Felix Nmecha fired wide in the 54th, a minute after Greece keeper Konstantinos Tzolakis had palmed a Joshua Kimmich free kick over the bar.
The Greeks, however, almost scored in the 66th after Kimmich lost possession in his own half but substitute Fotis Ioannidis fired just wide of the post.
They did better in the 74th with Kourbelis’ deflected low drive that gave them the win to make it two victories in a row after their last-gasp 2-1 win over Serbia on Thursday.
In the same group, Netherlands earned a 2-1 victory over Serbia thanks to Mexx Meerdink’s double strike on his second appearance for his country.
It was the first win under new coach Xavi Hernandez following their draw with Germany on Thursday.
“It’s a boyhood dream. I actually don’t have any words for it,” Meerdink said. “Everything is happening so quickly. You just don’t realise what can happen in the space of a week. It’s also great that we managed to win here.
“Sometimes you need a bit of luck. This time it went my way. Then you have to be there and be important for the team. I did feel a little pressure, I was a bit nervous. But you play that out of your system. And then to be allowed to score two is fantastic.”
Joao Felix scored for the second consecutive Nations League match as defending champions Portugal, with Cristiano Ronaldo on the bench throughout, edged past hosts Norway 2-1 to top Group A4 with two wins from two matches so far.
The Norwegians cancelled out Felix’s 17th-minute lead with Erling Haaland’s equaliser before Goncalo Ramos’ chip won it for the visitors.
Ben Davies scored a 53rd-minute own goal and Gustav Isaksen added another on the hour as Denmark eased past Wales 2-0 to earn their first points in Group A4.
In a politically charged encounter in Group B3, Ireland scored twice in three minutes early in the first half to ease past Israel 3-0.

briefs.headline: A bank that India can deep dive into in the Africas
briefs.deck: Perhaps now, the turnaround is imminent. Only time will tell, but watching Kuldeep run rings around the West Indian batters in Thiruvananthapuram on Sunday in the first ODI, you couldn’t help but wonder why successive team managements haven’t invested more in this now mature, seasoned 31-year-old.
briefs.bodyText:
Fast bowling is a very physically demanding and unnatural activity that places immense strain on various different parts of the body. The most affected, one might say, are the back, the knees and the ankles, but the shoulder bears a heavy burden too, as does the heel and the shin.
Fast bowling calls for sheer bloody-mindedness, especially in a country like India where, until perhaps a decade back, the pitches offered absolutely no assistance even in domestic cricket. The diktat to leave a few millimetres of grass, interestingly during Sourav Ganguly’s tenure as the BCCI president, has had a domino effect with the medium-pacers and those slightly quicker than that having a field day at the expense of spin. But even so, it requires a certain mindset to want to embrace fast bowling in the subcontinent – perhaps with the exception of Pakistan, who somehow seem to throw up quicks a dime a dozen.
It’s not as if spin bowling is an easier endeavour. It would seem to be an unequal contest, fast bowlers thundering in from 20 yards to hurl the cherry and the spinners trundling in from five or six yards – unless you were Derek Underwood or Ajantha Mendis – to let go of the ball. But anyone who thinks bowling spin comes easy clearly doesn’t understand cricket enough.
And it’s not as if spinners aren’t putting themselves at the risk of picking up injuries, either. The seam cutting against the inside of the forefinger and the middle finger triggers such pain and discomfort that oftentimes, it’s hard to even grip the ball and well nigh impossible to release it with the desired revs. But such is their devotion to their craft that the finger spinners make light of such terrible exigencies, determined to hoodwink batters in the air and off the surface while being mindful of how much the odds are stacked against them in modern-day cricket.
If the lot of quality finger-spinners is anything but straightforward, think of the wrist-spinner. There is arguably no other type of bowling that asks such probing questions as that of a wristie. For starters, they need to be encouraged to keep at it because a bad delivery is never far away, because such is the very nature of that craft. Especially in one’s formative years, it is very easy to get disheartened, and more so if encouragement isn’t forthcoming from coaches, captains, parents and peers. But even when one establishes themselves at the highest level, the gremlins of self-doubt never disappear completely.
Shane Warne might have made leg-spin look glamorous and ridiculously easy with his larger-than-life persona and a supreme command over how the ball left his hand but hey, how many wrist-spinners have taken 700 Test wickets? Or even 700 wickets in first-class cricket? Warne was the striking exception, the genius touched by greatness long before he made an eminently forgettable Test debut in Sydney in January 1992 against India. Figures of one for 150 – his lone success was double-centurion Ravi Shastri – were hardly flattering, but Warne wasn’t the only to show that it isn’t how you start, but how you develop and finish, that matters the most.
Generous with inputs
Warne wasn’t just a great bowler, he was also generous with his inputs and advice, with his learnings and wisdom. In international cricket, they talk of a fast bowlers’ club, and a spinners’ club. For a long time, the latter was populated by three of the most successful tweakers of all time – Warne, Sri Lankan giant Muttiah Muralitharan (Test cricket’s highest wicket-taker with 800 scalps) and our own Anil Kumble, with the temperament of a fast bowler and the heart of a champion that often took the sheen away from his not inconsiderable skillset.
It was probably little less than providential that two of these three members contributed to a rookie left-arm wrist-spinner – the term Chinaman is frowned upon these days, apparently because it is politically incorrect – announcing himself on the world stage more than nine and a half years back. Kumble was India’s head coach for only one year – more the Indian team’s loss than the towering Bengalurean’s – but that was time enough for him to bequeath to Indian cricket that great rarity in the history of the game, a left-arm wrist-spinner.
Through the first three of Australia’s four Tests in India in early 2017, Kuldeep Yadav was steadfastly ignored by Virat Kohli. An unfortunate shoulder injury to the captain forced him to miss the decider in Dharamsala – the series was tied 1-1 – and Ajinkya Rahane, the stand-in skipper, heeded his coach’s words and opted to throw the 22-year-old from Kanpur into the deep end.
Master’s advice
His first bowl is what we tend to call a ‘dream debut’. On a decidedly pacer-friendly day-one strip at the HPCA Stadium, he made Australia’s batters dance to his tune. Kumble had facilitated a conversation between Warne and Kuldeep before the match, and while English may not have been the latter’s strongest suit at the time, he showed that language is hardly a barrier when it comes to cricket by putting the master’s advice to great effect.
His first Test wicket was that of David Warner, with a flipper that Warne had talked about in detail. Then followed the sticks of Peter Handscomb, Glenn Maxwell – coming off a century in the previous game in Ranchi – and Nagpur as Kuldeep finished with four for 68 from 23 outstanding overs. A start had emerged, you told yourself, a star for whom the sky was the limit.
Kuldeep’s career has, as has been well chronicled, not taken off along expected lines. Nine and a half years after that stirring debut, he has only 19 Test caps. Somehow, he has been the most expendable of the spinners, ostensibly at the altar of batting depth. For a type of bowler who relies on confidence, trust, encouragement and backing, to be forced to look over his shoulder and wonder if he will get a second Test on the trot isn’t the ideal base from which to perform, as former India leg-spinner Narendra Hirwani agreed during a conversation with this writer a couple of weeks.
Pigeonholed more as a limited-overs bowler – 122 ODIs and 54 T20Is for 198 and 95 scalps respectively – Kuldeep has plugged away manfully in the two shorter formats. He must be hurting immensely at not playing more Tests, even on home patch, and sometimes, that feeling of hurt and maybe not being wanted has manifested itself in scratchy, underwhelming performances that infuriate because one knows that Kuldeep is capable of much, much more.
Turning a corner?
Perhaps now, the turnaround is imminent. Or perhaps, even now, that could be a false dawn. Only time will tell, but watching Kuldeep run rings around the West Indian batters in Thiruvananthapuram on Sunday in the first ODI, you couldn’t help but wonder why successive team managements haven’t invested more in this now mature, seasoned 31-year-old.
Put in on an excellent batting strip, the Caribbeans seemed on course for a total in excess of 350 on the back of sterling opening stand of 135 between Justin Greaves and John Campbell in just 19.2 overs. Enter Kuldeep, so send them tumbling to 198 for five, including wickets in successive deliveries of Greaves and Jewel Andrew, who had no answer to a ripping wrong ‘un that caught the splice of his bat and lobbed to Rohit Sharma at slip.
Kuldeep finished with four for 40, his best ODI figures since September 2023, when he took five for 25 against Pakistan in the Asia Cup in Colombo. Only thrice subsequently in the next 34 ODIs until Sunday did he manage a four-wicket haul, but there was something different about how the ball left his left hand in Thiruvananthapuram.
Flow and confidence
The pace was optimal, the control impeccable, the rhythm very, very evident. It certainly helped that he got a wicket early on because more than anyone else, Kuldeep thrives on flow and confidence, and once he realised that he was hitting the areas that he was targeting, he appeared so dangerous as to threaten a wicket almost every delivery.
Kohli produced another one of his trademark centuries in a chase, seeing the team home by eight wickets with plenty to spare, and Shubman Gill dazzled with a pleasing hundred of his own, but there truly was only one candidate for the Player of the Match award.
Kuldeep had single-handedly downscaled the West Indian total by at least 50 runs and while there is no gainsaying what the outcome would have been even if Shai Hope’s men had touched or crossed 350, the wrist-spinner pulled the chase down to little more than ordinary proportions with his mesmeric presence at the bowling crease.
Not the best of times
Across formats, Kuldeep hasn’t had the best of times of late. He hasn’t taken more than two wickets in a T20I innings for 12 months, while the last of his five five-fors in Test cricket came in October last year, also against West Indies. His last five bowls in the five-day game have brought him just four successes in 54.5 overs and he had a forgettable Galle Test last month, finishing with match figures of one for 103 from 25 overs as he was comprehensively shaded by finger-spinners Manav Suthar and Ravindra Jadeja.
Kuldeep has found himself at a crossroads so often in his nearly decade-long international career that he must experience a sense of déjà vu whenever he is pushed to a corner. He has found a way to spring back several times, and one can only hope that Sunday is a seminal moment in that it will lead to a sustained expression of tricks and sleight of hand.
Over the next week, in the next two ODIs, and in the five T20Is to follow, he will get further opportunities to build on this grand start to the home season. If he can snare a bagful of wickets, it will put him in an excellent state of mind as India head to New Zealand in three weeks’ time for their first full tour there since January 2020.
Kuldeep is the kind of bowler who can make a decisive impact even on pitches that don’t offer him much help, a bank India will hope to dip into at the 50-over World Cup in the Africas in 12 months’ time.
For long, Kuldeep himself has been his worst enemy; that’s something he and the think-tank must work assiduously to arrest as Indian cricket enters an exciting phase pregnant with glorious possibilities.

briefs.headline: Chess Olympiad: Gukesh and Savitha stand out for India
briefs.bodyText:
There was no repeat of the glory of Budapest, but India’s men and women managed to climb the podium nevertheless.
India had arrived in Samarkand as the defending champion in both the open and women’s sections of the Chess Olympiad. In 2024, India had indeed created history with a show that underlined its status as a powerhouse in the mind game.
So the expectations about India retaining both the crowns were high. And the country had players to do the job. Yes, there were concerns about the form of D. Gukesh. But, the World champion opted to play on the fourth board, and not on the first, which he did at Budapest and before that at home in Chennai (Mamallapuram) in 2022.
He was brilliant in both those tournaments and won the individual gold medal, too. He clinched silver this time around, and contributed significantly to his team. A loss in the final round, in the match against Hungary notwithstanding, he showed what he is capable of.
With his World title match against Javokhir Sindarov coming up in a couple of months’ time, he should be in a better frame of mind now than he was before the Olympiad got underway.
Another player from Chennai, B. Savitha Shri, must be feeling even better. She won individual gold as the reserve player and remained unbeaten. More importantly, she struck for the women’s team almost as if on demand. She would either win or at least draw whenever her team needed.
It is no small feat to win eight out of the 10 games at an Olympiad. Savitha has always shown promise. Now she seems to be ready for bigger things. This could be a turning point in her career.
Savitha wasn’t the only member of the Indian women’s team to win an individual medal. Koneru Humpy, Divya Deshmukh and the often underrated Vantika Agrawal also excelled on their respective boards. The only one to miss out was R. Vaishali.
Her younger brother R. Praggnanandhaa claimed bronze in the open section. He had the difficult task of playing on the top board. But the Indian team management’s decision to assign him for the games against the strongest players at the Olympiad was hardly surprising. He had been in fantastic form.
But, it wasn’t the perfect Olympiad for him. Just as it wasn’t for India, but that is because the bar keeps rising for Indian chess.

briefs.headline: Indian cricket, in terms of fast bowling, is in good hands: Prasidh
briefs.bodyText:
Prasidh Krishna, like all aspiring cricketers of his generation, grew up watching Virat Kohli bat.
On Sunday night at the Greenfield Stadium here, the Indian quick got to watch from the dressing room the master conjuring up an extraordinary knock.
“It was unbelievable,” he said, echoing just about everyone who witnessed that stunning assault by Kohli in the first ODI, which India won with more than eight overs remaining.
“Sitting outside, we were thinking, what do we bowl to him at that moment? He was striking the ball really, really well. We were all excited.”
Prasidh too contributed to the Indian win, claiming two wickets. And he has been having a good time with the white ball; he is India’s leading bowler in ODIs this year with 15 wickets from eight matches.
“Every single session we go in, we are looking to improve at something,” he said. “And every game poses a different kind of challenge. When you come in knowing what exactly must be done, there is clarity within the team, there is clarity in me as to what I do when I come in. There is enough communication going on. All this helps me bowl well.”
Competition
About the competition in pace-bowling slots in the Indian team, he said: “It is great. We are seeing a lot of fast bowlers coming in. It is really good for the Indian cricket team, honestly. You keep pushing each other.
“And every time we go into nets, we know the kind of bowlers that we’re bowling amongst. I would say Indian cricket, in terms of fast bowling, is in good hands”.

briefs.headline: Asian Games 2026: Yashvir, Gulveer, and Sreeshankar capture silver
briefs.deck: Rohit makes it a double podium for India in javelin; Vithya breaks the National record en route her third-place finish in 400m hurdles; Parul bags a bronze for the second successive day; Sable ends fourth in 3,000m steeplechase
briefs.bodyText:
A National record was broken and some personal marks were bested at the Paloma Mizuho Athletics Stadium as the Indians added more medals to their kitty on Monday (September 28, 2026), of both hues except the golden one the country desperately craved.
Three years ago, Vithya Ramraj ran the 400m hurdles in 55.42 seconds, equalling the longest standing Indian track record held by the legendary P.T. Usha for 39 long years since 1984. It helped her top the group before eventually winning bronze in Hangzhou. On Monday (September 28), the 28-year-old won another bronze but this one was a lot more special — the 54.75 seconds finally made her the sole National record holder, in the presence of Usha, now the IOA president. Anu Raghavan, meanwhile, also ran an individual best 55.88 seconds to finish fifth.
If Vithya found herself in elite company, the javelin throw continued to be the country’s reliable medal-earners with India managing a double podium finish. In Neeraj Chopra’s absence, Rohit Yadav and Yashvir Singh were expected to shoulder the burden and both stepped up on the big stage.
Yashvir, in particular, justified his last-minute inclusion as Neeraj’s replacement, throwing 85.72m for a personal best and silver. Yashvir went hard to match up to leader Rumesh Pathirage but the Sri Lankan world leader and pre-tournament favourite dug deep in wet and challenging conditions for 88.55m in his final throw and won the gold. Rohit managed 84.35m for bronze.
Gulveer Singh, too, added a second silver to his tally here with a new personal mark of 3:36.72s in the 1500m — after leading for more than 1.5 laps and looking set for the top spot before Kazuto Iizawa overtook him in the final 20m. Long jumper M. Sreeshankar, too, got his second silver in as many Games with an effort of 8.07m.
Unfortunately, the constant downpour meant the track and the take-off board were extremely slippery and Sreeshankar’s left leg slipped dangerously in his fourth attempt, the 27-year-old landing awkwardly on the pit and twisting his ankle. He skipped his last two attempts but the second jump was good enough to ensure him the second spot behind China’s Shi Yuhao’s 8.17m.
India missed out on a podium for the first time in 32 years in women’s discus throw. Seema Kaliramna’s personal best of 59.88m fetched her only a fourth position. Seema, who had won bronze at the Commonwealth Games recently, was unable to emulate another Seema (Punia), a legend of the sport with five consecutive medals from 2006-2022.
The biggest upset, however, was defending champion and favourite Avinash Sable finishing fourth in 8:21.67s in the 3,000m steeplechase. It was only his second race this year and a far cry from the Games record of 8:19.50 last time around. Parul Chaudhary took home a second bronze in the 5,000m.
